newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed hopes sacking boosts presidency bid. [CORRECTED 10:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed hopes sacking boosts presidency bid. [CORRECTED 10:45 GMT]

text.p: Alexander Lebed's dethroning as Russia's security tsar looked less like a setback on Friday than a stride towards a more glittering crown -- the presidency.

Hours after his dismissal by President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday, Lebed was back on the attack against his Kremlin rivals, warning them of a "hot autumn" and declaring his intention to become president in his booming bass voice.
His confident and vigorous display was a stark contrast to Yeltsin's haggard look and stiff movements as he told television viewers he was sacking his former protege.

It also highlighted the fact that Yeltsin may unwittingly have boosted Lebed's presidential hopes by making him a martyr to an administration which is led by an ailing president and remains deeply unpopular.
"I was a born winner. Sooner or later, victory will be mine," the 46-year-old reserve general warned his rivals last June. That declaration sums up his thinking today.

Yeltsin and his aides realise Lebed's potential as an opposition leader and must have considered it before sacking him. But they appear to be banking on the 65-year-old president remaining in power for a reasonable length of time.
The Kremlin's best hope of blunting Lebed's threat is that Yeltsin recovers from a heart bypass operation scheduled for next month.
Their other choice would be to keep him in power as a figurehead for as long as possible if doctors decided he was too ill for the operation.

Kremlin aides hope that the longer Lebed is in opposition, the less impact his attacks will make. They are sure to attack the reserve general, and the media are likely to continue a vicious campaign against him.

Lebed's best hopes of becoming president rest on an early poll. He is popular, his rivals would have little time to prepare their bids and, in Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's case, little chance to improve their public image.
But it is not yet clear if he would find wealthy backers able to bankroll his quest for power.

Humiliated by the president signing his dismissal order with the television cameras rolling, Lebed is in a similar position to Yeltsin when Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev ruthlessly swept him aside and gave him a public dressing down in 1987.
"Alexander Lebed is a very popular man with the people. And, speaking openly, I think he is like the Boris Yeltsin of 1987," said Boris Nemtsov, governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region.
Like Yeltsin, Lebed is dangerous when he is down and has a measure of public support. Lebed, a boxer in his youth, wrote in his autobiography: "When a cat is cornered, it becomes a tiger."

Few Russians can have forgotten how Yeltsin returned to humiliate Gorbachev when, live on television, he ignored Gorbachev's protests and signed a decree (Corrects to make clear that Yeltsin signed the decree, not Gorbachev) temporarily banning the Russian republic's Communist Party.

Some Russian politicians and political analysts say Lebed deliberately contrived to get himself sacked to distance himself from the Kremlin and portray himself as a victim of political intrigues. Russians traditionally sympathise with underdogs.
"He had been trying to get himself dismissed for quite a long time. That is clear," Sergei Parkhomenko, editor of the current affairs magazine Itogi, said in a television interview.
"He knowingly broke all the rules of the game which existed in the (Kremlin) team."
Lebed's main achievement in four months in the Kremlin was the deal he signed on August 31 to end fighting in Chechnya.
If fighting erupts again, Lebed is sure to say he alone in Moscow was responsible for establishing peace and blame the collapse of the ceasefire on the policies of his Kremlin rivals.
Such comments would be likely to boost his standing with ordinary Russians, most of whom are weary of the conflict.
Lebed has not said how he will fight now he is out of the Kremlin. He could create his own political group or remain independent.
Lebed could also try to revive the campaign team which helped him to third place in the first round of the presidential election last June with 11 million votes.
But he achieved that success with the help of Yeltsin's team in the final stages. How it would work in complete opposition to the Kremlin is uncertain.
